newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanon threatens radical Shi'ite leader.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon threatens radical Shi'ite leader.

text.p: President Elias Hrawi, warning that lawlessness and chaos could not be tolerated in postwar Lebanon, threatened legal action against a radical Shi'ite Moslem cleric who has called for civil disobedience by the poor.
Hrawi told a late-night cabinet meeting on Wednesday the call for a "hunger revolt" by Sheikh Sobhi Tufaili, a former head of the pro-Iranian Hizbollah (Party of God), was a threat to state security.
Those threatening the interests of the country and its security "shall be legally pursued", Hrawi was quoted as saying.
No one in Lebanon had "carte blanche" to say or do what they pleased and the country was not a political podium for those wishing to threaten friendly countries, he said.

Tufaili has threatened to lead a march on Beirut from the predominantly Shi'ite eastern Bekaa valley next month to launch a civil disobedience campaign if the living conditions of the poor are not improved.
He said people in the Bekaa were desperately hungry and demanded free schooling and hospital treatment, reduction of income tax and exemption from electricity and water bills for the poor.

Information Minister Bassem al-Sabaa quoted Hrawi as telling the cabinet Tufaili was making "clear threats to state security and the safety of citizens and threatening the interests of Lebanon and its relations with a friendly country".
Security agencies had detected a flow of weapons to "known forces" in the Bekaa, Hrawi said.
"It is not acceptable that anyone calls for resisting the government by threatening all kinds of lawlessness practised years ago," Sabaa quoted him as saying.

Tufaili led Hizbollah in the 1980s but no longer holds any post in the movement. He has long been linked in the Arab media to Iranian hardliners and has sharply criticised the present Hizbollah leadership for what he calls "a wavering incoherent policy of appeasement".

The Bekaa valley, which is controlled by Syrian troops, has suffered economically from a crackdown on illegal drug crops which flourished during the civil war. Residents complain the government has failed to support profitable alternative crops.
Hrawi also objected at the cabinet meeting to threats made in Beirut by an anti-Turkish Kurdish rebel on Monday against Turkey, the United States and Israel.
"Lebanon has taken a stance on the Turkish aggression on Iraqi soil but this does not mean it is a carte blance for individuals or parties to act as they please on Lebanese soil," Hrawi said.

This was a reference to a news conference on Monday in a Hizbollah suburb of Beirut at which an official of the Kurdish Workers Party (PKK) threatened attacks on the United States, Turkey and Israel in retaliation for Turkey's campaign against Kurdish rebels in northern Iraq.
